name: Nora Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Nora, and thank you for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's a small hill farm, Top Rigg, forty hectares of steep grass that my father farmed before me. Ivan and I keep thirty-five suckler cows, that's beef cows that rear their own calves, and we make hay on the two flat fields by the river. This time of year I'm feeding silage in the morning, checking the water troughs haven't frozen, then doing the books at the kitchen table in a paper diary. What I like is the quiet up there, and what wears me out is that the money never quite stretches to the end of the month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is the farm all of your income?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ivan does some hedge-cutting for neighbours with the old tractor, that's a bit extra. Otherwise yes, the calves are our income, and we sell them at the autumn sale in town. There's the land, of course, but you can't eat land, and we've never had more than a few weeks of money in the bank. I don't have a computer, my son set one up once and I gave it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there we are, then. I wouldn't make a fuss either way, I'd just say it at the mart over a cup of tea, that it was a lot of talk. I'm not online, so no one would hear it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean nothing for us, and I'm glad of that. We farm the same way my father did, more or less, and the cows don't care about computers. The thing on my mind is the price of feed and the calf price at the autumn sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as I am. Feed, calve in spring, make hay in summer, sell in autumn. I wouldn't buy anything and I wouldn't learn anything, because there'd be nothing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast said rain and it rained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything on your farm use AI or computers now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cattle passport records go in online now, so my son does them on his phone when he visits. I write it in the diary, he types it in, and the government gets it twice as fast as it did when I posted it. That's the only computer this farm needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be thinking about instead, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether either of the children wants the farm. Neither does, really. That's the real question for the next ten years, not machines.

S0.say: I'd say there we are, it was a lot of talk, and I'd say it over tea at the cattle market. I'm not online, so nobody would hear it there.
S0.think: It'd mean nothing for us and I'm glad. My mind is on feed prices and what calves fetch at the autumn sale.
S0.do: Carries on her farm year exactly as before: feeding, calving, haymaking and selling at the autumn sale. Buys nothing new and learns nothing new.
S0.feel: Calm, as if the forecast said rain and it rained.
S0.quote: I write it in the diary, he types it in, and the government gets it twice as fast as it did when I posted it.
S0.fieldNote: Nora runs her farm by a paper diary and her son types the records in for her. She doesn't take sides on AI; she just expects nothing from it. The question she actually carries is succession, since neither child wants the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one brings more change. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, some do well and some don't. I wouldn't blame anybody, farming has always changed. I'd say it to the neighbours and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it would mostly pass us by, at least at first. It's the big flat farms down the valley that would get the robots, not a hill place like ours. But I worry it makes their beef cheaper than ours, and then what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait. I'd watch what the bigger farms do for a couple of years before I did a thing. Maybe I'd let my son put whatever app the auction mart wants on his phone for us, but that's as far as I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think robots could even work on land that steep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen the quad bikes roll on that bank, so I'd like to see a robot try it in February. Maybe one day. Not in the years I've got left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the calf price, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Down, probably, if the big farms can make beef cheaper. A hundred less a calf and we're short for the winter. We'd manage, we always have, but it'd be a thin year.

S1.say: I'd say it's how things go, some do well and some don't, and farming has always changed. I'd tell the neighbours and leave it.
S1.think: It would mostly pass us by because robots would go to the big flat farms first. But their beef might get cheaper than ours.
S1.do: Waits a couple of years to watch what bigger farms do before changing anything. Lets her son install whatever app the auction mart asks for, and nothing more.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, without losing sleep.
S1.quote: I've seen the quad bikes roll on that bank, so I'd like to see a robot try it in February.
S1.fieldNote: Nora's steep land feels like a shield to her, and she may be partly right in the short run. Her real exposure is price, not her own job, which she understands clearly. She blames nobody; change is weather to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very fast. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I hope somebody in charge knows what they're doing. I wouldn't march or anything, it's not me. But I'd want to know what happens to people like us before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think this is where small farms get finished off. Not because a robot takes my job, I'm my own boss, but because big robot farms make beef so cheap ours isn't worth rearing. And with two years there's no time to find something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything to the bone that first year, no new tractor tyres, no holiday, which we never have anyway. If prices dropped, I'd sell the river field to the neighbour who's been asking for years, to keep us afloat. And I'd talk to my son about whether we can lean on him for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I wouldn't panic, that's not how I'm made, but I'd be worried for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling a field. Which one, and how would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The river field, it's the best hay. Dad bought that field the year I was born, and I'd be the one who signs it away. I'd hate it, but land's the only savings we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ivan about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we sell the field and keep the house and the rest. He'd say we can manage without selling, he always does. We'd argue, then I'd go and do what I said.

S2.say: I'd say I hope someone in charge knows what they're doing, and I'd want to know what happens to people like us. I wouldn't march, that's not me.
S2.think: This is where small farms get finished off, not because a robot takes my job but because cheap robot-farmed beef makes ours worthless. Two years leaves no time for anything else.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the bone in the first year and sells the river field to a neighbour if prices drop. Asks her son whether they can lean on him for a while.
S2.feel: Anxious and worried for herself and Ivan, but not panicking.
S2.quote: Dad bought that field the year I was born, and I'd be the one who signs it away.
S2.fieldNote: Being self-employed changes the shape of her fear: she worries about prices, not being replaced. Land is her only savings and selling her father's field is the concrete cost. Her steadiness keeps her from alarm, and she has a clear, unglamorous plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same, with more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I'd say I hope they plan it. With five years, there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan for small farms. I'd say it to whoever came round asking for votes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would get me to sixty-three and Ivan to sixty-five. That's near enough to stop, I think. But the calf price would start dropping before the robots were even here, I'd bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start letting some of the land to the neighbour on a grazing agreement, slowly, so it brings in rent. We'd cut the herd from thirty-five down to twenty over the five years. And I'd put the rent money aside, which would be the first savings we'd ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but a slower worry. More like a long winter than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning any of the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not learning a machine to compete with a machine, I'd rather let the land to someone who does. That's just honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the house? Would you stay at Top Rigg?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to die there, if I'm honest. Let the land, keep the house and the garden and a few cows to look at. That's the plan, if the money lets us.

S3.say: I'd say I hope they plan it, and with five years the government has no excuse not to have a plan for small farms. I'd say it to anyone asking for votes.
S3.think: Five years gets me to sixty-three and Ivan to sixty-five, near enough to stop. But I'd bet calf prices start falling before the robots even arrive.
S3.do: Lets some land to a neighbour for grazing, bit by bit, to earn rent. Cuts the herd from thirty-five to twenty over five years and puts the rent aside as savings.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a slow worry like a long winter rather than a storm.
S3.quote: I'm not learning a machine to compete with a machine, I'd rather let the land to someone who does.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Nora wind down rather than sell, which matters a lot to her. She flatly refuses to learn the technology but is happy to let someone else use her land. The grazing rent would be the first savings they've ever had, which says a lot about their position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen. I wouldn't make speeches about it. I'd just say we'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, ten years is fine. We'd be retired by then, more or less. It's for the young ones to sort out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are for now. Somewhere around 2030 we'd let the land and keep a few cows. I'd keep writing in the diary and let my son do the computer side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mainly for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-eight. Would you still have cows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few, for the company. A cow is better company than a robot and she doesn't need charging. Ivan would keep the tractor going until it fell apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandson, he's twelve and he wants to farm. I don't know what I'd tell him. Learn the robots, I suppose, though it would stick in my throat to say it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen, so we'll see. I wouldn't make speeches about it.
S4.think: For us ten years is fine, because we'd be more or less retired by then. It's for the young ones to sort out.
S4.do: Carries on farming as now and plans to let the land around 2030 while keeping a few cows. Keeps her paper diary and leaves the computer work to her son.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly on behalf of others.
S4.quote: A cow is better company than a robot and she doesn't need charging.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts AGI past her working life, and she relaxes into a slow handover. The only real worry is her twelve-year-old grandson, and advising him to learn robots would ‘stick in her throat’. She stays in the middle: no blame, no politics, just patience.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We're not frightened of losing the work, we're frightened of the work not being worth anything. What would help is a fair price for calves from small farms, some kind of floor on it, and help for older farmers to retire without selling the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hills. If the small farms go, who keeps the walls up and the bracken down? Somebody should think about that before it happens.

headlineQuote: We're not frightened of losing the work, we're frightened of the work not being worth anything.
portrait: Nora Petrov is a 58-year-old hill farmer who keeps thirty-five beef cows on forty steep hectares she inherited from her father, farming with her husband Ivan. They have almost no cash saved, and the land is their only wealth. She keeps her books in a paper diary, never uses AI and doesn't want to. She is practical and blames nobody; she sees change as weather. She is calm or uneasy about slower change, anxious about fast AGI because cheap robot-farmed beef could make her calves worthless, and with more time she plans to let the land and wind down.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because large robot farms could make their beef worth so little that they'd have to sell land.
whatWouldHelp: A floor on the price of calves from small farms, and help for older farmers to retire without selling their home.
